note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §7, §13.7, Stage 87; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiments 37 and 39) on data/benches/crystal_violet.json: crystal violet fading in base, read by absorbance at 590 nm. Hydroxide in a thousandfold excess makes the second-order fading first order in the dye: ln A falls linearly in time, its slope -k' = -k2 [OH-]. Two runs side by side at 0.030 and 0.015 M hydroxide, at one ionic strength, give the order in hydroxide and k2.
title: Experiment: crystal violet, a first-order decay

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: Crystal violet's cation takes a hydroxide ion onto its central carbon and loses its colour. Halve the hydroxide: how does the rate the violet fades at change? Write the order in hydroxide you expect (1: half as fast; 2: a quarter as fast).

steps.title: Blank the first spectrophotometer
steps.text: Both spectrophotometers read at 590 nm, where the violet absorbs most. Put the cuvette of water in the first one's well and blank it: what the water and the glass absorb reads 0.

steps.title: Blank the second
steps.text: Take the water out of the first well and put it in the second one's, and blank it too.

steps.title: The dye in both wells, held at 25 C
steps.text: Set the water aside. A cuvette of crystal violet in each well, and each holder on at 25 C: the rate depends on the temperature, so both runs are held at one.

steps.title: Warming to 25 C
steps.text: The holders warm the dye from the room's 20 C.

steps.title: The hydroxide in, stirred
steps.text: Pour each tube into its cuvette, all of it, and stir both: t1's 0.12 M hydroxide makes c1 0.030 M, t2's 0.06 M makes c2 0.015 M. t2 also holds 0.06 M sodium chloride, so both stand at the same ionic strength: ions slow a reaction between oppositely charged ions (the salt effect), the same in both.

steps.title: Log both absorbances
steps.text: Log each spectrophotometer's absorbance every 5 seconds: the notebook keeps them in time.

steps.title: The violet fades
steps.text: Wait for both to read under 0.15. In the notebook, plot each log against time with y as ln: two straight lines, the steeper at the more hydroxide.

report.label: k' at 0.030 M hydroxide
report.why: In the notebook: spec1's absorbance against time, y as ln, fit: the slope is -k'. A first-order decay, A = A0 e^(-k' t), its half-life ln 2 / k'.

report.label: the order in hydroxide
report.why: n = ln(k' at 0.030 / k' at 0.015) / ln 2. The rate is k2 [CV+] [OH-]: half the hydroxide, half the rate. At one ionic strength the salt effect is the same in both runs; without the sodium chloride the weaker run would be a tenth faster than half, and the order would read low.

report.label: k2
report.why: k2 = k' / [OH-], 0.00592 / 0.030. At 25 C and an ionic strength of 0.03; Begum et al. measured 0.234 at 0.007, where the salt effect slows it less.
